newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl convinced tax reform is in sight for 1997.
newsitem.headline: Kohl convinced tax reform is in sight for 1997.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Thursday he was convinced that cross-party bickering over tax reform would give way to an agreement this year.

"I have no doubt that we will come to an agreement (on tax reform) this year," Kohl a press conference with trade unions and business to launch a new jobs pact for former communist east Germany. "At the latest it will come before the mediation committee meetings this summer."

Kohl's assurances came days after the Bundesrat upper house of parliament, dominated by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), voted down a bill intended to reform Germany's tax system and stimulate investment and jobs creation.
The reforms, backed by Kohl's ruling coalition, will be addressed again this summer, probably in July, by a mediation committee charged with hammering out a compromise between the two sides.
Kohl's Christian Democrats have proposed cutting corporate taxes to 40 percent from 45-47 percent and slashing the top 53 percent rate of income tax.
Kohl has said sweeping tax reform is urgently needed to boost investment across the country and reduce post-war record levels of unemployment in Germany.

But SPD-ruled states say that government plans to cut taxes are not balanced by plans to increase revenues elsewhere, a sensitive issue after Bonn announced last week it faced an 18 billion mark tax revenue shortfall.
